details:
**If on a winter's night a traveler**
Calvino's 1979 metafictional novel, which opens "You are about to begin reading Italo Calvino's new novel." The odd-numbered chapters are told in the second person and follow "You, the Reader," who keeps finding that the book he has started is defective or unfinished. The even-numbered chapters are the opening chapters of ten different novels, each of which breaks off at a moment of suspense.

**Ludmilla**
The "Other Reader," a woman the Reader meets in a bookstore when he goes to exchange his defective copy of the book. They chase the missing novels together, and the book ends with the Reader and Ludmilla married, reading in bed side by side.

**Ermes Marana**
A fraudulent translator and literary forger who founds the Organization of Apocryphal Power. He deliberately splices together and falsifies manuscripts, which is why the Reader can never finish any book. He is driven by jealousy of Ludmilla, who was once his lover, and the Reader follows his trail to the revolution-torn country of Ataguitania. One novel he "translates" is Looks Down in the Gathering Shadow, credited to the fictional Bertrand Vandervelde.

**Professor Uzzi-Tuzii and Cimmeria**
Uzzi-Tuzii is a university professor and the last remaining expert in the literature of Cimmeria, a fictional and now vanished country. He identifies one of the interrupted novels as the Cimmerian Outside the town of Malbork. In the novel Cimmeria was absorbed by its neighbor Cimbria, and rival scholars argue over which country a text belongs to.

**Silas Flannery**
A blocked Irish thriller writer in If on a winter's night a traveler, whose diary forms one chapter. He watches a woman (Ludmilla) reading through a telescope, thinks about copying out Crime and Punishment word for word, is visited by UFO enthusiasts, and is told that a computer could finish his novel In a network of lines that enlace.

**Invisible Cities**
Calvino's 1972 book, framed as conversations between the Venetian traveler Marco Polo and the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. Polo describes 55 imaginary cities, all named after women, and arranges them in categories such as "thin cities," "hidden cities," "continuous cities," "cities and memory," and "cities and the dead." The two men at first communicate through gestures and objects, without a common language.

**Individual Invisible Cities and "something about Venice"**
Polo admits that "every time I describe a city I am saying something about Venice." Frequently clued cities include Diomira (with sixty silver domes), Octavia (a spider-web city strung across a chasm), Theodora (where exterminated creatures return), Melania (whose people keep playing stock dramatic roles), and Argia (filled with earth instead of air). The book also contains the line "it is not the voice that commands the story: it is the ear."

**Cosmicomics and Qfwfq**
A 1965 collection of whimsical stories, each starting from a scientific fact about the universe. Most are narrated by Qfwfq, an ageless being who has existed since the beginning of the universe and taken many forms. He returns in the follow-up collection t zero. Other stories include "At Daybreak" (in which Granny Bb'b recalls when matter was uniformly scattered), "Without Colors" (in which the narrator's love Ayl flees when colors appear), and "The Aquatic Uncle" (about a fish relative who refuses to leave the sea for land).

**"The Distance of the Moon"**
The first story of Cosmicomics. When the Moon was very close to the Earth, people rowed out to the Zinc Cliffs and used ladders to climb up and gather "Moon-milk," a kind of cheese. Qfwfq loves Mrs. Vhd Vhd, but she loves his deaf cousin, who is the best at the task. She ends up stranded on the Moon as it moves away from the Earth.

**"All at One Point"**
A Cosmicomics story set when all matter in the universe was packed into a single point. Mrs. Ph(i)Nk₀ generously cries that she would love to make them all some noodles, and that wish to make room for kneading pasta sets off the Big Bang.

**The Baron in the Trees**
Part of Calvino's Our Ancestors trilogy. In 1767, twelve-year-old Cosimo Piovasco di Rondò refuses to eat a dish of snails cooked by his sister Battista and climbs into the trees, vowing never to come down. He spends the rest of his life there, has a love affair with Viola, and finally vanishes by grabbing the rope of a passing hot-air balloon, so no body is ever found. The story is narrated by his brother Biagio.

**The Cloven Viscount**
The first novel of Our Ancestors. Viscount Medardo of Terralba is split in half by a cannonball during a war against the Turks. The two halves return separately as a cruel "Bad 'Un" and a sickeningly virtuous "Good 'Un," who duel over the peasant girl Pamela and are finally sewn back together.

**The Nonexistent Knight**
The third novel of Our Ancestors, about Agilulf, a paladin of Charlemagne who is an empty suit of white armor held together only by willpower and devotion to rules. He saves the maiden Sofronia, and his squire Gurduloo is his opposite, a man with a body but no sense of self.

**The Path to the Nest of Spiders**
Calvino's 1947 debut novel, about the Italian partisan resistance in World War II. The orphan Pin, whose sister is a prostitute called "the Dark Girl of Long Alley," steals a pistol from a German sailor who is one of her customers and hides it at a secret place where spiders nest. Jailed, he meets the young Communist partisan Red Wolf, then joins the ragtag band of the commander Dritto, who betrays the unit by sleeping with the cook's wife. At the end Pin befriends the partisan known as Cousin.

**Mr. Palomar**
Calvino's last novel (1983), made up of short meditations by Mr. Palomar as he tries to observe the world precisely. Famous scenes include his watching a gecko on the glass of his terrace from below so that its insides are visible, his trying to "read" a single wave, and his trips to the zoo, where he watches an albino gorilla.
